full_judgment:
4. The learned Assistant Judge upon considering the evidence in the case, by his judgment and decree dated 25.1.1984. decreed the suit on contest against defendant no.1 with cost and ex-parte against the rest without cost Principal defendant no. 1 was directed to execute and register a sale deed in favour of the plaintiff in respect of the suit land within 60 days from the date of the decree failing which the plaintiff was given the liberty to execute the decree through Court. It was also directed that "the plaintiff must deposit the balance consideration price of Tk. 3,000/- by 15.2.1984 failing which the suit shall stand dismissed. The decree was, however actually signed by a Subordinate Judge-in-Charge on 8.3.1984. 

 10. Leave was granted to consider whether there has been a miscarriage of justice on account of the failure of the learned Subordinate Judge and also of the learned Judge of the High Court Division to notice that the judgment in question was admittedly delivered on a date which is not shown in the Court's own record, namely, the daily cause list and as such the plaintiff-appellant had no occasion to know about the same. 

 13. Order XX Rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that when the judgment is not to be pronounced on some future day, the Court shall fix a day for that purpose, of which due notice shall be given to the parties or their pleaders. Admittedly the judgment in the present case was not delivered after the hearing of the arguments on 12.1.1984 and the date for judgment was fixed on 22.1.1984 which is clear from the certified copy of the 'daily cause list' (Annexure "A to the revision petition). In the daily cause list of 22.1.1984 the matter did appear for judgment but evidently the judgment was not delivered as the matter appeared for judgment again in the 'daily cause list of 6.2.1984. 

 14. Rule 1 the Civil Rules and Orders (Volume 1 Part I Chapter 1) provides that a Daily Cause List in the prescribed Form No. (M) 2 shall be posted in some conspicuous part in every Court-house for the information of the parties, their pleaders and the public. Cases a appeals shall be shown in the order in which they appear in the Diary. Note to the said Rule provides that judgments ready for delivery should be notified on the cause list for the day. Note 2 at the end of Rule 13 reads thus: Owing to the difficult known to be experienced maintaining the lists as laid down above the Supreme Court (High Court Division) favour the maintenance of a register in the same form in which the necessary entries shall be made from day to day and signed by the presiding Judges as indicated above. The register shall be laid at some conspicuous place in the court-room everyday at the special hours for inspection by parties and Advocates. 

 16. While granting leave we called for a report as to the incongruity between the order sheet of the Court (showing delivery of judgment on 25.1.1984) and the 'daily cause list' as on the record and a report has been submitted by the present incumbent of the Court concerned from which it appears that not only the 'daily cause list' but also the diary of the Court shows that the suit was set down for judgment on 22.1.1984 and 6.2.1984. The diary also shows that the judgment was delivered on 25.1.1984. It has been reported that the incongruity in question was perhaps due to the mistake committed by the concerned Bench Assistant who is not available now in the judgship of Narayanganj. Whoever may have been at fault the Court's own record shows that the plaintiff-appellant had no opportunity to know about the date of the judgment and there is nothing on record to show that he was otherwise aware of the same (25.1.1984) and admittedly the 'daily cause list' put the dates differently. In the facts and circumstances of the case we hold that there has been a clear miscarriage of justice by reason of non-consideration either by the learned Subordinate Judge or by the learned Judge of the High Court Division of a simple and apparent fact. The omission is such as cannot be adequately deplored. Mr. Shamsul Haque Chowdhury learned Advocate appearing for defendant-respondent No. 1, found himself unable to resist the grievance made by the plaintiff-appellant and we think he has been fair enough.
